query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Fine-tuning the elemental composition of an AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy by increasing its Al content and incorporating a controlled amount of Ti promotes the in situ formation of a coherent, adherent spinel oxide during friction at elevated temperatures, thereby enhancing its resistance to tribo-corrosion degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy with conventional (near-equiatomic) composition before deliberate adjustment of Al and Ti levels.
generation.intervention: Adjust the alloy composition by increasing the relative amount of Al and adding a modest, controlled addition of Ti to finely balance the reactive element ratio.
generation.conditions: Exposure to elevated temperature environments with simultaneous sliding or reciprocating wear in corrosive media (to simulate combined tribological and corrosive stresses).
generation.structural_mediator: The optimized reactive element content triggers the in situ formation of a protective spinel oxide layer that is coherent and adherent to the alloy surface during wear.
generation.mechanism: The formation of the spinel oxide acts as a self-healing, physical barrier that impedes both further mechanical wear and corrosive attack. This protective layer limits material loss and slows overall degradation by reducing diffusion and oxidation kinetics at the alloy surface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional alloys or a non-optimized AlCoCrFeNi HEA, the modified alloy is predicted to exhibit reduced wear depth and lower corrosion rates under identical high-temperature tribo-corrosion conditions, leading to enhanced durability.
generation.baseline: Conventional structural alloys and unmodified AlCoCrFeNi-based HEAs that do not achieve controlled, in situ formation of a protective oxide layer under elevated temperature tribo-corrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected within a specific temperature window where spinel oxide formation is favored, and its performance might diminish if temperatures or corrosive conditions fall outside this experimentally defined regime.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal concentration ranges of Al and Ti needed to reliably form the desired spinel oxide under diverse tribo-corrosion conditions remain to be determined. There is also uncertainty regarding the long-term stability of the oxide layer under cyclic stresses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one set of the optimized AlCoCrFeNi alloy (with increased Al and added Ti) and one set of the baseline alloy. Subject both sets to controlled tribo-corrosion testing in a high-temperature chamber (e.g., 700–900 °C) under sliding contact in a corrosive environment. Characterize surface oxide formation using in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) and electron microscopy, and measure wear depth and corrosion rates over time.
measurements: Corrosion rate (e.g., mass loss over time)
Oxide layer thickness and morphology (via electron microscopy and XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized HEA does not display a statistically significant reduction in both wear depth and corrosion rate, or if the anticipated coherent spinel oxide layer either fails to form or exhibits poor adhesion compared to the baseline material, then the hypothesis that composition fine-tuning enhances tribo-corrosion resistance via spinel formation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. decision.trend: Early HEA studies primarily focused on mechanical strengthening and high‐temperature oxidation/corrosion resistance by engineering microstructures (e.g., via powder metallurgy, spark plasma sintering, and additive manufacturing) and incorporating ceramic reinforcements. Around 2019, research such as in PMC7515071 began investigating the wear behavior of AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 in reciprocating tests at elevated temperatures, revealing that, under high-temperature conditions, the in situ formation of a spinel oxide helped decrease the wear depth. Although significant progress was made in understanding mechanical degradation and passive film formation separately, few studies have directly targeted the coupling between tribological wear and corrosion (tribo‐corrosion) in such HEAs.
decision.unsolved: The synergistic mechanism of in situ oxide (spinel) layer formation during sliding contact at high temperature, and how optimized composition can reliably trigger and stabilize this protective scale under combined tribological and corrosive stresses, remains insufficiently addressed.
decision.lever: Fine-tuning the balance of principal elements—specifically adjusting the Al and Ti contents in the AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA—to promote the controllable in situ formation of a coherent and adherent spinel oxide during wear at elevated temperatures
decision.why: This lever builds directly on the observed trend that spinel formation (as seen in PMC7515071) can enhance wear resistance at high temperatures, addressing the current gap in achieving durable tribo‐corrosion resistance. By tailoring the composition to optimize the reactive element ratio, one can target the formation of a self-healing protective oxide, which follows logically from the prior attempts and the design cues for extreme environment performance.
